title: Schemas, code generation, and why they matter
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain what a schema-based protocol buys over hand-written parsing, evolve a schema without breaking existing callers, and say when this machinery is worth its cost.

blocks.text: The capstone protocol was a length prefix and a body you parsed by hand. That works, and it stops scaling the moment several teams and several languages depend on it — because the format lives in each implementation's code rather than in one place both sides agree on. A schema moves it to that one place.

blocks.caption: A definition both sides compile against
lines: string id       = 1;      // the number is the field's identity on the wire
int64  cents    = 2;      // the NAME is not sent; only the number is
rpc Watch (WatchRequest) returns (stream Order);   // a stream of results

blocks.text: From that file, a generator produces types and client and server stubs in each language that needs them. Neither side writes parsing code, and neither side can drift from the contract without the file changing — which is the actual benefit, more than the encoding.

blocks.title: The field numbers are the wire format
blocks.text: Only the numbers travel; the names exist for humans and for generated code. That is why renaming a field is harmless and changing its number is a breaking change — the receiver looks up 2, not 'cents'. It is also why the encoding is compact: no field names on the wire, and integers encoded in as few bytes as their value needs.

rows: Add a new field with a new number
Old receivers ignore what they do not know
Yes, if the number is never reused
Old senders may still send it; it is ignored
Reuse a removed number for something else
An old sender's data is read as the new field
Some documented conversions share a wire type; a change to an incompatible wire type is unsafe
Both sides stop agreeing about what anything is

blocks.title: Reusing a retired number is the one that corrupts data silently
blocks.text: Removing field 2 and later adding a different field as number 2 means an old sender's value is parsed as the new field's type. There is no error — the bytes are valid, they simply mean something else now. Reserve retired numbers explicitly so the generator refuses to reuse them, which is exactly the kind of mistake a schema is supposed to prevent.

rows: A remote call looks like a method call
Many messages in one call, either direction
A budget passed with the call

blocks.text: Every row rests on something from earlier in this course. Multiplexing is why one connection carries many calls without the queuing that HTTP/1.1 had. Deadlines are the mechanism the RPC lesson said a chain of calls needs. And because it is HTTP/2 underneath, the connection is one you now know how to inspect.

items: A build step: the generator must run, and generated code must stay in step with the schema
Opacity: the traffic is binary, so you cannot read a capture without a decoder
A learning cost for everyone who touches the interface
Weaker fit for browsers and for public interfaces, where plain HTTP and JSON are the expectation

blocks.title: Choosing honestly
blocks.text: For internal service-to-service traffic with several languages and a schema that will change, this machinery pays for itself quickly. For a public interface, a small internal tool, or a single-language system, plain HTTP with JSON is usually the better answer — it is readable in a capture, debuggable with curl, and needs no build step. The measure is whether the contract has enough consumers to be worth formalising, not whether the technology is modern.

You began with two machines and a wire, and you now have a working TCP server written three ways, a diagnostic method for each layer, and a view of what the frameworks above are actually doing. A gRPC call is a request and a response, serialised according to a schema, multiplexed over an HTTP/2 connection, carried by TCP, routed by IP, and delivered by a link layer that resolved a hardware address to reach the next hop. Every one of those is a lesson in this course, and you can now inspect each of them independently when something goes wrong.

blocks.title: Compare the two approaches on your own protocol
steps: Prerequisite: protoc and a gRPC code-generation plugin for your language. If they are not installed, this lesson still stands alone as reading — come back to the hands-on part once they are
Write a schema describing the message your capstone server exchanges
Generate code for it in the language of your choice and write a client against the generated stub
Capture the traffic with tcpdump and compare its readability with your hand-written protocol
Add a field to the schema, regenerate only the client, and confirm the old server still works
Now change an existing field's number, regenerate, and observe the failure
Remove a field, reuse its number for a different type, and observe that data is silently misread
Add the reservation that prevents that, and confirm the generator now refuses
Finally, list the parts of your system where JSON over HTTP would be the better choice, and say why for each
blocks.expected: A working generated client, a compatible change and two incompatible ones you caused deliberately, and a reasoned list of where you would not use this. That last item is the point of the lesson: the goal is to choose between the two with a reason, not to adopt whichever is newer.

cheatsheet: A schema puts the message format in one place both sides compile against
Field numbers are the wire format; names are for humans and generated code
Safe: add a field, rename a field, remove one whose number is never reused
Unsafe: reuse a retired number, change a type, renumber a field
Reserve retired numbers so the generator refuses to reuse them
gRPC adds generated stubs, streaming, deadlines and status codes over HTTP/2
Multiplexing means many calls share one connection and one handshake
Costs: a build step, binary traffic you cannot read directly, a learning curve
Plain HTTP with JSON is usually better for public interfaces and small systems

checkpoint.prompt: You rename a field in the schema and regenerate both sides. What happens to compatibility?

choices.A: It depends on the field type
choices.B: It breaks only for old clients
choices.C: Nothing breaks — only the field number travels
choices.D: It breaks — the name is part of the wire format

checkpoint.explanation: Names exist for humans and generated code. That is also why changing a number is a breaking change while changing a name is not.

checkpoint.prompt: Field 2 was removed a year ago. A new field is added and given number 2. What goes wrong?

choices.B: The old field's bytes are parsed as the new field
choices.D: Nothing — the removed field no longer exists in the schema

checkpoint.explanation: The bytes are valid; they simply mean something else now. Reserving retired numbers is what makes the generator refuse this, and it is precisely the mistake a schema exists to prevent. It happens silently and without any error.

checkpoint.prompt: Why can gRPC carry many concurrent calls over one connection without them queuing behind each other?

choices.B: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one connection
choices.C: Calls are batched by the client
choices.D: It opens a new connection for every call it makes

checkpoint.explanation: This is the HTTP/2 property from the HTTP lesson, applied. It also means one handshake serves many calls, which is the connection-reuse benefit measured there. gRPC runs on HTTP/2, which is what carries independent streams over a single connection.

checkpoint.prompt: When is plain HTTP with JSON the better choice?

choices.B: Never — a schema is always the more professional choice
choices.C: For public interfaces and small systems

checkpoint.explanation: The measure is whether the contract has enough consumers to be worth formalising. A readable, curl-debuggable interface with no build step is a real advantage where those conditions do not hold. Think public interfaces, browser clients and small single-language systems: readability and no build step outweigh the schema there.
